title: Rethinking the Lawyers' Monopoly: Access to Justice and the Future of Legal Services
pub: Cambridge University Press (edited volume); Introduction, pp. 1–22
author: David Freeman Engstrom · Nora Freeman Engstrom

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source does not directly endorse the cluster’s central claim that human oversight must provide effective control through independent verification and preserved expertise. Instead, it reframes the priority around unmet legal need and whether professional restrictions should yield to direct-to-consumer AI, while leaving consumer safety unresolved.
qs: If, as Deborah Rhode astutely observed two decades ago, “[w]hat Americans want is more justice, not more lawyering,” it is incumbent on us to rethink how the current professional monopoly impacts the supply of necessary legal services.[Footnote 24](#fn24)  The other tectonic force fueling skepticism about the lawyers’ monopoly is the coming of new technologies, particularly AI.
Should technologies that generate legal advice be reserved for use solely by attorneys, or can they be safely put directly into consumers’ hands?

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source treats AI-driven legal disruption primarily as an access-to-justice and regulatory-monopoly question, redirecting attention from law-firm leverage, junior revenue and apprenticeship. Although it anticipates augmentation and automation of legal services, it provides little evidence on pyramid restructuring, employment, training or pricing.
qs: If, as Deborah Rhode astutely observed two decades ago, “[w]hat Americans want is more justice, not more lawyering,” it is incumbent on us to rethink how the current professional monopoly impacts the supply of necessary legal services.[Footnote 24](#fn24)  The other tectonic force fueling skepticism about the lawyers’ monopoly is the coming of new technologies, particularly AI.
Should technologies that generate legal advice be reserved for use solely by attorneys, or can they be safely put directly into consumers’ hands?

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source does not assess whether junior pipelines face the sharpest workforce risk or whether broad lawyer displacement is occurring. Instead, it reframes AI’s significance around access to justice, direct-to-consumer legal services, and reconsideration of lawyers’ professional monopoly and regulation.
qs: If, as Deborah Rhode astutely observed two decades ago, “[w]hat Americans want is more justice, not more lawyering,” it is incumbent on us to rethink how the current professional monopoly impacts the supply of necessary legal services.[Footnote 24](#fn24)  The other tectonic force fueling skepticism about the lawyers’ monopoly is the coming of new technologies, particularly AI.

Indeed, the advent of generative AI holds the promise that the millions who currently go without any legal help at all can enter plain language descriptions of a legal problem into a machine and receive back actionable information and advice.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source shifts the emphasis from lawyer-supervised AI and verification burdens to reconsidering lawyers’ regulatory monopoly so that AI may directly serve consumers and substitute for some provider functions. It acknowledges consumer-safety uncertainty, but does not develop the cluster’s substantive verification and lifecycle-control framework.
qs: If, as Deborah Rhode astutely observed two decades ago, “[w]hat Americans want is more justice, not more lawyering,” it is incumbent on us to rethink how the current professional monopoly impacts the supply of necessary legal services.[Footnote 24](#fn24)  The other tectonic force fueling skepticism about the lawyers’ monopoly is the coming of new technologies, particularly AI.
Should technologies that generate legal advice be reserved for use solely by attorneys, or can they be safely put directly into consumers’ hands?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not directly establish the cluster’s task-level, jagged-capability account of legal AI or its emphasis on verification and workflow redesign. Instead, it reframes AI chiefly as one force intensifying the access-to-justice crisis and the case for reforming restrictive legal-services regulation, while treating safe consumer deployment as unresolved.
qs: This collision – the access-to-justice crisis hitting up against the growing presence of legal tech, all on top of a creaky and restrictive regulatory regime built in an earlier, analog era – leaves the lawyers’ monopoly on increasingly thin ice.
Should technologies that generate legal advice be reserved for use solely by attorneys, or can they be safely put directly into consumers’ hands?

st.t: Regulatory sandboxes: Conditional entry tests consumer risk
st.an: The source documents distinct state liberalisation efforts and organised resistance, supporting the cluster’s account of uneven, jurisdiction-specific reform. But it neither evaluates sandbox oversight nor takes a clear position on whether conditional entry can reduce unmet need without unacceptable consumer risk.

st.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
st.an: The source documents substantial federal self-representation and identifies UPL rules as a consumer-access barrier, but it does not assess whether GenAI caused increased filings, improved litigant outcomes, or shifted screening and verification costs to courts and opponents. Its position on the cluster’s principal proposition therefore cannot be determined.
qs: 231, 238–39 (2021) (“Of some 260,000 civil cases filed annually [in the federal courts], about twenty-five percent are brought by people without lawyers, and more than half the cases before the federal appellate courts are brought by self-represented parties.”).
28 *See, for example*, [Footnote *id.*](#fn27) at 8 (explaining that UPL laws present an obstacle to putting legal tech products in the hands of consumers).

st.t: Effective help: Justice outcomes outrank lawyer supply
st.an: The source accepts that closing the justice gap requires more than increasing lawyer supply and materially develops the cluster’s practical reform agenda through a field-specific method: identify the distinctive needs of each legal domain and design narrow, tailored interventions. Its family-law proposals illustrate alternative combinations of lawyer, nonlawyer and procedural assistance, while remaining proposals rather than demonstrated justice outcomes.
qs: Aviel’s methodological exploration of the family law market for legal services – one that begins with an exploration of the substantive area of law at issue, followed by an identification of entry points for possible narrow-gauge reforms – presents a compelling model for stakeholders eager to jettison a transsubstantive framework and think through tailored reforms in other specific areas of the law.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core distinction between lawyer augmentation and partial task automation, while materially extending it into access-to-justice and professional-regulation questions. It argues that direct-to-consumer AI may substitute for some provider services and warrants reconsideration of lawyers’ regulatory monopoly, but treats safe consumer access and actual justice-gap reduction as unresolved rather than established.
qs: Should technologies that generate legal advice be reserved for use solely by attorneys, or can they be safely put directly into consumers’ hands?

st.t: Provider reform: Competition cannot overcome every access barrier
st.an: The source accepts that liberalising provider and ownership rules may help but cannot alone close the justice gap. It materially develops the cluster’s proposition by identifying weak consumer-market economics and by advocating people-centred, demand-side and problem-prevention measures alongside expanded providers, calibrated safeguards and institutional reform.
qs: Professor Michener authoritatively argues that “supply-side” reforms (e.g., increasing access to attorneys and funding for legal aid organizations) must be complemented with demand-side interventions, such as legislation to promote and empower the political organizing necessary to address legal problems at their source.

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s diagnosis that widespread self-representation coexists with severe unmet legal need and poor procedural outcomes, including defaults. Its evidence also identifies regulatory barriers to consumer legal technology without claiming that wider or cheaper AI access improves remedies, so it does not extend the cluster’s GenAI-specific causal or outcome analysis.
qs: Online 1, 8 (2021); *see* LSC Report, *supra* [Footnote note 14](#fn14), at 7 (“Low-income Americans do not get any or enough help for 92 percent of their substantial civil legal problems.”).

Online 146, 149 (2024) (explaining that “in many jurisdictions and in certain litigation areas – again, most prominently debt collection actions – the *majority* of lawsuits *never draw a responsive pleading* and, as a result, end in default judgment”).

st.t: Healthcare ownership: Financial gains do not prove patient benefit
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by citing healthcare studies associating private equity ownership with higher prices and adverse patient outcomes, undermining any inference that acquisition-related financial gains establish patient benefit. Its evidence is narrower and more uniformly negative than the cluster’s broader, measure-specific synthesis, and it does not address transferability to legal services.
qs: *supra* [Footnote note 43](#fn43), at 23–31 (finding that private equity acquisition of medical practices tends to be associated with significant price hikes and that increased prices “will eventually be paid by consumers in the form of higher health insurance premiums”); Singh & Whaley, *supra* [Footnote note 39](#fn39) (“[T]here is clear evidence that private equity ownership increases prices.”).

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central balance: direct-to-consumer AI may extend actionable legal help to people who otherwise receive none, but this remains a promise and safe consumer deployment is unresolved. It also aligns with reconsidering unauthorized-practice restrictions, without supplying evidence that direct use improves remedies or that users can manage verification risks.
qs: Indeed, the advent of generative AI holds the promise that the millions who currently go without any legal help at all can enter plain language descriptions of a legal problem into a machine and receive back actionable information and advice.
Should technologies that generate legal advice be reserved for use solely by attorneys, or can they be safely put directly into consumers’ hands?

st.t: Justice gap: Fair resolution exceeds legal assistance
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core claim that the justice gap is population-scale and cannot be closed merely by expanding conventional legal aid or lawyer pro bono work. Its account is narrower and more attorney-capacity-centred than the cluster’s broader fair-resolution framing, offering little evidence on recognition, trust, language or practical capability.
qs: Attorneys in the United States would need to increase their pro bono work from an annual average of thirty hours each to over *nine hundred hours each* to “provide some measure of assistance to all households with legal needs.”[Footnote 23](#fn23) Likewise, even a tripling or quadrupling of legal aid funding would barely be a drop in the bucket.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central framing: AI may expand access for people who currently lack legal help, but advice-generating tools challenge the lawyers’ monopoly and existing regulation, leaving safe direct-to-consumer use unresolved. It advocates reassessing provider restrictions without claiming that AI has already delivered effective or adequately protected access to justice.
qs: If, as Deborah Rhode astutely observed two decades ago, “[w]hat Americans want is more justice, not more lawyering,” it is incumbent on us to rethink how the current professional monopoly impacts the supply of necessary legal services.[Footnote 24](#fn24)  The other tectonic force fueling skepticism about the lawyers’ monopoly is the coming of new technologies, particularly AI.
Should technologies that generate legal advice be reserved for use solely by attorneys, or can they be safely put directly into consumers’ hands?

st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: The source supports access to legal help—not investment or market entry alone—as the purpose of liberalisation. It also identifies UPL reform, ownership reform and licensed nonlawyer-provider permissions as distinct regulatory developments. Its case is primarily normative and comparative, however, and it does not provide measured evidence that these reforms have reduced the justice gap.
qs: And it ultimately seeks to guide the market for legal services into a new, more accessible era.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on converting legal technology into responsibly delivered, accessible services rather than treating technical capability alone as sufficient. Its contribution is narrower and primarily regulatory: it frames the justice gap, UPL and lawyers’ monopoly as pressures requiring multidisciplinary, empirically informed reform, while offering neither a specific implementation model nor evidence on verification or task-specific evaluation.
qs: And if *change is coming*, one must then contemplate what that change will look like and how it can responsibly be ushered into existence.

By reframing the issues, infusing empirically minded expertise, and tapping a diverse array of stakeholders and disciplinary perspectives, the volume contributes to a growing and vital debate about what works, what doesn’t, and what lies ahead in the [next chapter](urn:cambridge.org:id:book-part:9781009528535%23bp3) of the civil justice system.

kp.k: Access pressures and technology challenge the lawyers’ monopoly
kp.d: The editors argue that the collision of unmet civil legal need and technology-powered delivery makes some regulatory change inevitable. They describe a historically restrictive combination of unauthorized practice of law (UPL) rules and lawyer-ownership requirements, while footnote 1 acknowledges exceptions for government, nonprofit and in-house practice. Their claim of impending transformation is a prediction and framing argument, not a measured finding about AI’s effects.
qs: First is mounting public concern about what many rightly see as an accessibility crisis in the American civil justice system. Second is the rise of new tech-powered legal service delivery models that seem capable of ameliorating that crisis.
This one-two punch has meant that only lawyers can provide legal advice and that even lawyers can’t practice law in nonlawyer-owned entities.

kp.k: Existing evidence documents extensive unmet civil legal need
kp.d: The introduction cites Sandefur’s 2016 estimate that as many as half of American households experience a significant civil justice situation at any given time. It reports that at least one party is self-represented in approximately three-quarters of 20 million annual state civil cases, citing 2015 and 2018 court research. The 2022 LSC report says funded organizations turn away half of requests because of limited resources and cannot provide any or enough help for an estimated 1.4 million problems brought to them annually. These are evidence supporting the access crisis, not findings that AI resolves it.
qs: as many as half of American households are experiencing at least one significant civil justice situation at any given time.
In approximately three-quarters of the 20 million civil cases filed in state courts each year, at least one side proceeds pro se.
Low-income Americans do not get any or enough help for 92 percent of their substantial civil legal problems.

kp.k: More lawyers alone cannot close the justice gap
kp.d: The editors reject exclusively lawyer-supply-based solutions. They cite Hadfield’s 2014 estimate that annual pro bono would need to increase from thirty hours to over nine hundred hours per attorney to provide some assistance to all households with legal needs. They also assert that even tripling or quadrupling legal aid funding would be insufficient. Footnote 30 reports approximately 30 percent growth in the profession since 2000 without a corresponding reduction in unmet need.
qs: Attorneys in the United States would need to increase their pro bono work from an annual average of thirty hours each to over *nine hundred hours each* to “provide some measure of assistance to all households with legal needs.”
Likewise, even a tripling or quadrupling of legal aid funding would barely be a drop in the bucket.

kp.k: Generative AI promises augmentation and direct consumer substitution
kp.d: The editors describe legal technology as supporting both lawyer augmentation and outright automation. They assert that generative AI already performs a growing range of higher-order legal cognitions and is entering direct-to-consumer tools that substitute for some provider services. Plain-language systems supplying actionable advice to people without help are presented as a promise, without task-level performance or safety measurements. Footnote 27 cites a 2024 landscape report noting a 30 percent rise in venture funding since 2021.
qs: Leveraging potent new forms of generative AI, legal tech tools can now perform a growing array of higher-order legal cognitions, supercharging how lawyers serve their clients.

Generative AI is also sweeping into “direct to consumer” tools that serve litigants directly and, in important ways, double for the services that lawyers or other legal services providers might offer.

Indeed, the advent of generative AI holds the promise that the millions who currently go without any legal help at all can enter plain language descriptions of a legal problem into a machine and receive back actionable information and advice.

kp.k: Consumer-facing and court-hosted AI raise unresolved regulatory questions
kp.d: The introduction asks whether legal-advice technologies should remain restricted to lawyers, whether consumers can use them safely, and whether courts should build generative AI assistance for self-represented litigants. It treats the application of UPL to private and court-hosted tools, and lawyers’ continued control over those decisions, as unresolved questions rather than offering a definitive legal or safety conclusion.
qs: Should technologies that generate legal advice be reserved for use solely by attorneys, or can they be safely put directly into consumers’ hands?
Should courts themselves create generative AI-driven tools to assist self-represented litigants?
In what circumstances does a legal tech tool, including a court-hosted one, run afoul of UPL laws?

kp.k: State liberalization faces substantial organized professional resistance
kp.d: The editors describe Arizona and Utah as opening legal services to outside investment and nonlawyer provision, alongside community justice worker programs and licensed paraprofessionals in jurisdictions including Colorado and Oregon. They contrast these developments with the ABA House of Delegates’ 2022 resolution discouraging nonlawyer fee-sharing, California’s 2022 closure of a reform working group, and Florida’s rejection of nonlawyer ownership proposals. The ABA’s stated concern about professional values is a reported opposing position.
qs: Arizona and Utah have led the charge, rewriting the rules around UPL and law practice ownership.
In 2022, for instance, the American Bar Association’s (ABA) House of Delegates passed, by a landslide vote, a resolution discouraging states from permitting lawyers to share fees with nonlawyers.
Such fee-sharing, the ABA intoned, is “inconsistent with the core values of the legal profession.”

kp.k: User-centered reform requires diverse providers and disciplinary perspectives
kp.d: Summarizing Sandefur and Burnett, the editors advocate replacing one-size-fits-all lawyer-centric reform with responses fitted to users’ identities, circumstances and preferences. Potential providers include paraprofessionals, community justice workers and Tribal lay advocates. The editors also recommend incorporating political economists, consultants and organizers into reform design rather than relying exclusively on lawyers.
qs: Empirical evidence, they point out, demonstrates that a vast number of individuals experience legal needs – and those needs are shaped by a range of factors, including gender, race, geography, and willingness to invoke or engage with law.
Depending on the person or problem, legal paraprofessionals, community justice workers, or Tribal lay advocates may be far better suited to offer assistance and support.
The profession cannot continue to turn only to attorneys for their perspectives and knowledge but must instead embrace political economists, consultants, union organizers, and more.

kp.k: Supply restrictions may amplify racial discrimination in representation
kp.d: The introduction reports Libgober’s prior field experiment, published in 2020, finding that requests using Black-sounding names received half the callbacks of those using white-sounding names. It summarizes his chapter’s mechanism: where attorney demand exceeds supply, lawyers can be more selective, worsening discrimination. The implication that expanding provider categories could reduce racial inequities is presented as his political-economy argument, not as an observed outcome of AI or regulatory reform.
qs: those with [B]lack-sounding names receive only half the callbacks of those with white-sounding names in response to requests for legal representation.
Restrictive rules that artificially constrain supply, it follows, may exacerbate racial inequities – and may further skew the allocation of legal assistance.

kp.k: Liberalization must address quality and public-facing professional duties
kp.d: Allensworth’s chapter argues that restrictive entry rules coexist with insufficient discipline: only some 500 of 1.4 million licensed practitioners were disbarred nationwide in 2021, and even permanent disbarment often permits petitions for reinstatement. She recommends stronger discipline alongside admitting qualified nonlawyers. Separately, Wendel uses hypotheticals to argue that reform must preserve judgment and duties owed to courts, the public and other lawyers; his concerns about nonlawyer performance are conceptual, not reported empirical findings.
qs: Only some 500 lawyers, total, were disbarred nationwide in 2021, out of 1.4 million licensed practitioners.
It militates not only in favor of an overhaul of the disciplinary system – to beef it up – but also in favor of a relaxation of those rules that lock even high-quality nonlawyers out.
Using hypotheticals, Wendel illustrates how nonlawyer providers may struggle to fulfill the “public side” of lawyering

kp.k: Direct-to-consumer legal technology faces a lifetime value trap
kp.d: The editors summarize Engstrom and Lu’s explanation for why rapid technological progress has not produced a robust consumer legal-tech market. UPL and outdated court systems may contribute, but the chapter theorizes that episodic use, low revenues and limited ability to purchase additional services are more fundamental constraints. Passive income streams and enterprise customers are proposed conditions for sustainable models. The authors question whether liberalization deserves scarce reform resources if it cannot generate a viable consumer marketplace.
qs: the “lifetime value trap”: The low revenue potential of a customer base that needs services only episodically and often only once and, in any event, has limited ability to pay for additional services or products.
They conclude that, in order to build sustainable business models, DTC legal tech may need passive income streams and enterprise-level customers.
reformers cannot pin their hopes for solving the access-to-justice crisis solely on evolving technologies.

kp.k: Field experience supports evaluation, organizing and complementary interventions
kp.d: Kuhl’s chapter examines Los Angeles Superior Court self-help education, online dispute resolution and the Gina traffic chatbot while preserving judicial neutrality; the introduction says results were mixed without providing comparative effect sizes. Steinkamp and DiDomenico recommend stakeholder engagement and quantitative and qualitative evidence in right-to-counsel reform. Michener’s accounts of tenant organizing argue for reducing the underlying power imbalances that generate legal problems, complementing rather than merely expanding service supply.
qs: LASC’s numerous efforts to improve services for pro se litigants – some of which were more successful than others – remind reformers to critically analyze interventions as they are put into place, always seeking to find room for improvement.

Collective action, she says, can ameliorate the power structures that *create* legal problems, like predatory landlords, exploitative employers, and the insufficient availability of affordable housing.

kp.k: Medical private equity offers a cautionary ownership analogy
kp.d: Hoffman’s chapter draws lessons from medicine’s opening to corporate ownership. The introduction reports nearly $1 trillion in private-equity purchases over the preceding ten years and cites studies associating ownership with increased costs and reduced quality. Footnote 45 reports an 11 percent mortality increase relative to controls in private-equity-owned nursing homes and a 25.4 percent increase in hospital-acquired conditions associated with hospital acquisition. These medical findings motivate caution about legal-services ownership reform; they are not findings about legal services.
qs: A battery of recent studies indicate that private equity investment in health care is associated with both a drop in quality and a rise in cost.
reporting that patients at private-equity-owned nursing homes suffered an 11 percent increase in mortality, as compared to controls
private equity acquisition was associated with a 25.4 percent increase in hospital-acquired conditions

kp.k: Medical adjuncts and Tribal advocates illustrate alternative provider models
kp.d: Peters’s chapter summarizes evidence that nurse practitioners and physician assistants deliver high-quality, cost-effective care, including in underserved areas. The introduction reports that non-M.D. providers perform over half of primary care visits and that nurse practitioners have full practice authority in most states, contrasting this with restrictions on independent nonlawyer advice. Van Schilfgaarde’s analysis of Tribal codes offers a distinct legal model: lay advocates are culturally knowledgeable, ethically accountable experts, not merely substitutes filling lawyer shortages.
qs: today, over half of primary care visits are performed by those without an M.D.
at lower cost than physicians and in under-served areas where it is difficult to recruit physicians.

This analysis reveals that Tribal lay advocates are not conceived of as a “gap-filler” for lawyers but are instead recognized as qualified, competent legal experts who are held to high ethical standards and are well-versed in the Tribe’s community, law, and culture.

kp.k: International experience qualifies technology-led and deregulation-led access promises
kp.d: Byrom argues that the Legal Services Act of 2007 did not deliver its anticipated technology-enabled access improvements in England and Wales; by 2023, the subsequent court technology program had spent most of its budget with only over half its projects completed. She questions participation incentives and unmet-need targeting in proposed public–private digital justice partnerships. Rühl describes German technology companies standardizing small consumer claims but argues that the Legal Tech Act of 2021 left lawyers more tightly regulated than those companies. The editors conclude that calibration and course correction matter.
qs: By 2023, the program had spent most of its budget with only over half of the planned projects completed.
But the Act, Ruhl says, failed to level the playing field between lawyers, who remain relatively tightly regulated, and legal tech companies, which continue to operate free from onerous requirements.
getting to a regulatory sweet spot may take time and a willingness to course-correct.

kp.k: First Amendment litigation could produce overly broad deregulation
kp.d: Lakier’s chapter considers Upsolve’s challenge to New York UPL restrictions on training nonlawyers to give free debt-collection advice. The introduction reports the 2022 trial-court ruling protecting the volunteers’ training and advice as speech, describing the case as still on appeal at the source’s writing. Although others welcomed the ruling as an access victory, Lakier warns that its reasoning could enable much broader invalidation of nonlawyer-practice restrictions. This is a prospective legal concern rather than an established consequence.
qs: Upsolve won the first round, as a trial court found that the training and advice provided by Upsolve’s volunteers constituted protected speech under the First Amendment.
Though still on appeal, many have hailed the trial court’s decision as a major win for access-to-justice advocates.
part of a sweeping “Lochnerization” of the First Amendment that could broadly deregulate the legal profession in ways that cause more harm than good.

kp.k: Hybrid federal regulation could support scalable legal services
kp.d: Engstrom and Rodriguez argue that the fifty-state regulatory patchwork mismatches increasingly national and global practice and discourages access-enhancing innovation. They propose retaining state oversight of conventional one-to-one lawyer and paraprofessional services while establishing federal oversight of entities delivering one-to-many services. Preserving local experimentation while enabling unified scalable delivery is the proposed benefit, not a demonstrated result.
qs: state bars would maintain regulatory control over conventional, one-to-one legal services provided by lawyers and paraprofessionals.
But a new federal regulatory authority would seize regulatory control of organizations and entities that furnish one-to-many services.

This approach, the authors contend, would retain the benefits of state experimentation and local knowledge, while enabling a more unified and efficient regulatory structure for modern legal services delivery.

kp.k: Tailored reforms may outperform uniform profession-wide changes
kp.d: Aviel argues that family law’s mandatory court involvement, sometimes aligned party interests and limited suitability for partisan advocacy justify considering joint representation, early neutral evaluation and nonlawyer family professionals. Issacharoff and Martin address institutional debt collectors’ advantage over unrepresented defendants through expanded advice providers, online dispute resolution and direct agency oversight, potentially led by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. These are proposed, domain-specific interventions, and the latter authors acknowledge limitations in each approach.
qs: Those distinctive attributes, Aviel posits, may require tailored interventions, including permitting joint representations, promoting early neutral evaluations, and permitting nonlawyer family law professionals to offer their services to divorcing spouses.

They propose several reforms to rein in these problematic lawsuits, including expanding the pool of individuals able to provide legal advice to defendants in these actions, utilizing online dispute resolution platforms, and, most prominently, direct regulatory oversight by state or federal agencies, perhaps led by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The editors describe generative AI as both augmenting lawyers and potentially substituting for some legal services directly to consumers, while emphasizing that technological progress alone does not ensure accessible or commercially sustainable services.
pts.d: David Freeman Engstrom and Nora Freeman Engstrom assert that generative AI already performs an expanding range of higher-order legal tasks and is entering direct-to-consumer tools that partly substitute for lawyers or other providers. They predict that people currently receiving no legal help could obtain actionable information and advice from plain-language descriptions of their problems. They also argue that emerging legal technology, combined with unmet civil legal need, puts pressure on the lawyer-controlled regulatory regime. This is a prediction about regulatory disruption, not a finding that AI has already eliminated the monopoly. In summarizing David Freeman Engstrom and Jess X. Lu’s contribution, the editors present a countervailing claim: rapid technological and AI advances have not produced a robust direct-to-consumer legal-tech market. Engstrom and Lu theorize that difficult customer economics, not merely UPL restrictions or outdated court technology, explain this weakness, and suggest that sustainable providers may need passive income streams and enterprise customers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The introduction offers literature references, funding trends, evidence of unmet legal need, and summaries of field-based arguments; it does not report AI performance benchmarks or measured AI-driven improvements in legal outcomes.
pts.d: For the growth of legal technology, the editors cite Megan Ma et al., Generative AI Legal Landscape 2024, noting a 30 percent rise in venture funding since 2021; they also cite that report for UPL obstacles to consumer-facing products. The access-to-justice rationale is supported by the 2022 Legal Services Corporation report and studies of self-representation, including the 2015 National Center for State Courts study. These establish unmet need rather than demonstrate AI effectiveness. The explanation of anemic direct-to-consumer provision is explicitly presented as Engstrom and Lu’s theory, grounded in their examination of providers and business models; the introduction supplies no quantified test of that explanation. Court self-help tools and comparative regulatory experiences provide contextual examples, but the text does not establish that all such tools use generative AI. No task-level accuracy, cost-saving, safety, or outcome measurements for generative AI are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Lawyer augmentation and the emergence of direct-to-consumer AI are described as current developments; widespread access benefits and regulatory transformation are prospective, without a specified deadline.
pts.d: Writing in the 2025 introduction, the editors use present-tense language for AI capabilities and consumer-tool adoption, but describe assistance for millions of unserved people as a promise. They leave unresolved whether advice-generating tools can safely be supplied directly to consumers, whether courts should create them, and how UPL rules apply. The predicted access benefits are qualified by the need for sustainable business models, appropriate regulation, and attention to market incentives. Engstrom and Lu’s suggestion that providers may need passive income streams and enterprise customers is conditional, not an established requirement. Their analysis also raises the possibility that liberalizing practice rules will not be sufficient to produce a competitive consumer legal-tech market.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central beneficiaries envisaged are unrepresented people with unmet civil legal needs; lawyers, consumer legal-tech providers, courts, and regulators face changes in service delivery and regulatory responsibilities.
pts.d: Low- and moderate-income Americans and self-represented litigants could obtain actionable assistance without retaining a lawyer, although limited ability to pay and episodic demand constrain commercial provision. Lawyers are described as receiving AI augmentation while facing partial substitution of their services by direct-to-consumer products; the introduction does not quantify employment displacement or predict particular staffing changes. Consumer legal-tech providers face regulatory barriers and customer-revenue constraints, potentially pushing them toward enterprise customers or other income sources. Courts face choices about hosting generative-AI self-help tools, and state bars and other policymakers face pressure to reconsider who may furnish legal advice and how technology-enabled services should be regulated. Enterprise customers appear as a potential source of business-model sustainability, not as the main access-to-justice beneficiaries.
